claims.text: Recruitment is the process of identifying that the business needs a new employee and attracting suitable people to apply for the vacancy; internal recruitment fills the vacancy with a candidate who already works for the business, while external recruitment attracts candidates from outside it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Selection is the process of choosing the candidate who best fits the vacancy from the people who applied, using tools such as application forms, interviews, references and, for some roles, practical tests.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A well-designed selection method, such as a structured interview or a practical test, tends to improve the fit between the person appointed and the job, because it gathers evidence the business can check against what the role actually requires.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Recruitment and selection carry costs as well as benefits: advertising, agency fees and management time are spent before any output is produced, and a poor appointment is likely to mean repeating the whole process.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal recruitment fills a vacancy with an existing employee, advertised through a staff notice or internal vacancy list, whereas external recruitment reaches people outside the business through job adverts, an employment agency or online job sites; the boundary between the two is whether the candidate already works for the business.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal recruitment is likely to be quicker and cheaper than external recruitment because the candidates are already known and no advertising to strangers is needed, and it tends to motivate other staff who see promotion routes open; but it leaves another vacancy to fill and brings in no fresh outside ideas.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: External recruitment widens the pool of candidates and can bring new skills and fresh ideas into the business, but it tends to be slower and more expensive than internal recruitment and carries a higher risk that the appointee does not fit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The main stages in recruiting and selecting an employee are: identify the vacancy and draw up a job description and person specification; advertise the vacancy internally or externally; receive and shortlist applications; interview and test shortlisted candidates; take up references; appoint the chosen candidate; and induct them into the role.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Each stage of the recruitment and selection process feeds the next: the job description and person specification set the criteria the advert states, the advert determines who applies, shortlisting applies the criteria to the applications, and the interview tests the shortlist, so a weak early stage tends to weaken every stage that follows.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A person specification is the list of the skills, qualifications, experience and personal qualities a business believes a candidate needs to do a particular job well; it is the criterion a business can use to decide which applicant to employ.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Deciding who to employ usually means weighing candidates or contract forms against each other: an internal candidate against an external one, or a part-time appointment against a full-time one, with cost, skills, availability and fit as the criteria the recommendation depends on.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The cheapest candidate is not necessarily the best appointment: skills and reliability usually matter more than a small wage difference where the role directly affects quality or customers, so the decisive criterion is which candidate best covers the work the vacancy exists to do.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A part-time employee works contracted hours that are fewer than the business's normal full-time hours, while a full-time employee works the full contracted week; the boundary is contracted hours, not how busy the days are or how long the job lasts.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Part-time employees tend to give a business flexibility - staffing can be matched to busy periods without paying for quiet ones - and openings appear for people who cannot work full time; but part-time cover can mean more people to train and communicate with, and handovers between them can let things slip.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Full-time employees tend to give a business continuity - the same people present most days, easier teamwork and more time to learn the role - but they cost more per person than part-time cover when demand is uneven, and off-peak hours still have to be paid for.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Training is the process of teaching an employee the knowledge and skills needed to carry out their job to the standard the business requires; induction training introduces a new employee to the business during their first days.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Training tends to benefit a business because employees who know what they are doing work faster and make fewer mistakes, which lowers wasted material and rework and tends to keep customers; it also eases the adoption of new technology and promotes from within, so fewer external recruits are needed for senior posts.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Training tends to benefit employees because it raises the skills they carry to future jobs and the pay those skills can command, and being invested in tends to raise their motivation, though training done at the employer's expense may come with an expectation of staying.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Training carries costs alongside its benefits: it takes time away from production, it costs money to deliver, and a newly trained employee is more attractive to other employers, so retention is part of the calculation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Induction training happens in the first days of employment: it introduces the new employee to the people, procedures and rules of the business, which tends to settle them in faster but carries little new-skill depth; on-the-job training is learning while doing the real job at the normal workplace, which is directly relevant but passes on existing habits along with skills; off-the-job training happens away from the workplace, often at a college or training centre, which brings up-to-date expertise but costs time away and travel.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The best training method tends to depend on the need: rules and people are learned by induction, day-to-day practical skill is often learned on the job, and broader or safety-critical skills often need off-the-job training, so most businesses mix methods.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Dismissal is when an employer ends an employee's contract because of the employee's own conduct or capability, whereas redundancy is when an employer ends a job because the role itself is no longer needed - the work is disappearing, not the person's behaviour; a fair dismissal has a valid reason and a fair procedure, and the boundary between the two ideas is where the cause sits.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An example of dismissal is a warehouse assistant dismissed for repeated lateness after warnings; an example of redundancy is the same warehouse assistant's job ending because a new scanning system removed the need for a second assistant - the person has done nothing wrong in the second case.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Redundancy, retirement and dismissal are three different exits: redundancy ends a job that is no longer needed, retirement ends working life at an agreed age, and dismissal ends a contract for a reason connected with the employee - confusing them matters because an employer who dresses a dismissal up as a redundancy is likely to face a claim of unfair dismissal.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Downsizing is a deliberate reduction in the size of a workforce, usually to cut costs; it becomes necessary in situations such as when falling demand for the product leaves more workers than there is work for, when new technology does work with fewer people, when costs must be cut to survive, or when a part of the business is closing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The reason downsizing situations arise is a mismatch between work and people: if demand for the product falls, fewer workers are needed to make it, and if a machine does the work of several people, those people are surplus to the output required - keeping them means paying wages the revenue no longer covers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A redundancy recommendation is judged against criteria such as which roles the remaining work actually needs, the skills each employee has and can retrain into, cost saved against redundancy pay, and legal fairness - but the employee whose contribution is most distinctive, because their skills or customer relationships are hardest to replace, is likely to be the one worth retaining even at higher cost.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Choosing whom to make redundant on cost grounds alone is risky: the cheapest employee to release may also be the one who holds the skill the remaining work depends on, so the recommendation depends on which skills the work still needs, not only on relative wages.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Employment law controls are the rules a government places on the relationship between employers and employees; the IGCSE syllabus names five areas: employment contracts, unfair dismissal, discrimination, health and safety, and the legal minimum wage.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Legal controls over employment tend to protect employees - a written contract, protection from dismissal without a fair reason, equal treatment regardless of personal characteristics, safe working conditions and a wage floor - but their details differ from country to country, so an IGCSE answer states what they aim at rather than quoting one country's law.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Legal controls raise business costs - wages at or above the legal minimum, safety equipment and training, and procedures before any dismissal - and businesses that respect them tend to gain trust, but the specific rules and enforcement differ by country.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Advertising a job vacancy is a stage of recruitment aimed at people who might apply to work for the business, telling them the job, what it requires and how to apply, whereas advertising a product is part of marketing aimed at customers and tries to persuade them to buy; the test is whether the reader is being asked to apply for a job or to buy something.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: External recruitment brings a new person into the business from outside to fill a vacancy, whereas off-the-job training, sometimes called external training, develops someone who already works for the business by teaching them away from the workplace; the test is whether the business gains a new employee or a better-skilled existing one.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A job description describes the job - its title, duties, responsibilities and who the post-holder reports to - whereas a person specification describes the person wanted for it - the skills, qualifications, experience and qualities needed; the job description is written first and the person specification is written from it, so a line describing a task belongs in the first and a line describing a quality of the applicant belongs in the second.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A temporary employee is employed for a fixed period or a particular task, whereas a part-time employee works fewer contracted hours each week than the business's full-time week; the two describe different things - how long the contract lasts and how many hours a week are worked - so an employee can be full-time and temporary, or part-time and permanent.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
